newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end little changed, mkt mood sours.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end little changed, mkt mood sours.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended little changed in active trade Thursday as the market failed to keep strong early gains tied to the release of a market-friendly retail sales report for November, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond closed up 2/32 at 98-12/32 after trading up as much as 1-2/32 in the first two hours of the session. Its yield was at 6.62 percent.
The 5.625-percent two-year note was up 1/32 at 99-22/32, yielding 5.79 percent.
Moods in the market turned sour as some major players continued to liquidate long positions, analysts said.
Flows were active. Analysts said at least one large mid-western hedge fund was seen as a major seller of Treasuries in the middle of the yield curve.
Portfolio managers were seen selling future bond contracts in an effort to hedge long positions in the cash market and lock their profits ahead of the end of the year.
"We saw a lot of people in the market today ... Though retailers were not perceived to be very active," said a money market trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Wall Street pundits said the recent drop in prices hinted that a change in the market's underlying sentiment, which was predominately bullish until about a week ago, has taken place.
"The only conclusion we can come to now is that the sentiment has changed 180 degrees," said Chris Rupkey, vice-president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

Analysts said the selloff, which was first seen as a technical adjustment, is now perceived to be tied to a growing sentiment in the market that the economic fundamentals might not be as soft as once thought.

Although no one seem to expect a booming economy going into 1997, market participants said tight labor markets, corroborated by a drop in jobless claims data released Thursday, are still indicative of a healthy economy.

"I think the outlook for growth is great looking down the road ... We're probably going to three percent GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth before we go to one percent GDP growth," BMT's Rupkey said.
Initial jobless claims fell by 317,000 in the week ended December 7 from a revised 330,000 in the prior week. The four-week moving average fell to 332,000.

A 0.3 percent rise in the November consumer price index was mostly in line with expectations. The core rate, which excludes food and energy price fluctuations, was up 0.2 percent. In October overall CPI also rose 0.3 percent.
The big pleasant surprise of the day in terms of economic data came from a sharp 0.4 percent drop in retail sales in November. The ex-autos number rose 0.3 percent.

"I don't think the market really belong, given the fundamentals, below 6.5 percent (in terms of yields on the benchmark 30-year bond)," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
The year bill rate was down two points at 5.18 percent.
The five-year note traded up 3/32 at 98-31/32 to yield 6.12 percent. The ten-year note closed up 2/32 at 100-28/32, yielding 6.38 percent.
Analysts said heavy issuance of corporate debt also dragged Treasury prices down. Traders said companies issued over $1.0 billion in fresh supply on Thursday alone.
Volume as measured by GovPX was $97.5 by late afternoon mostly in line with an average autumn Thursday.
GovPX publishes real time Treasury prices and volume from five of the six intra-dealer brokers, representing 65 percent of the intra-dealers trades.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down two basis points at 4.82 percent. The six-month bill rate fell five points to 4.98 percent.
